summary: Describes how to use the AES cipher in Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) as an authenticated encryption method for TLS 1.2. GCM provides both confidentiality and data origin authentication and is efficient in hardware and software. The document defines the TLS cipher suites that use it, with RSA key exchange and Diffie-Hellman variants.

plainLanguage.summary: This says how a web connection can scramble data and also check nobody tampered with it, using one fast method for both jobs, like a lock that also has a tamper seal.

questions: what is aes galois counter mode in tls
what is aes gcm in tls
what is a gcm nonce in tls
which tls versions support aes gcm cipher suites
subtitle: Twelve TLS 1.2 cipher suites that encrypt and authenticate each record in one step with AES in Galois Counter Mode.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.2 added authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) ciphers, but there were no cipher suites that used AES in Galois Counter Mode, which can be implemented efficiently in hardware and software.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines twelve cipher suites that use AEAD_AES_128_GCM and AEAD_AES_256_GCM with RSA, DSA and Diffie-Hellman key exchanges, builds a 12-byte nonce from a 4-byte salt and an 8-byte explicit part, and picks the SHA-256 or SHA-384 PRF.
tldr.outcome: Servers and clients that support TLS 1.2 can negotiate AES-GCM, which gives confidentiality and data origin authentication. The RFC has been updated by RFC 9325 and RFC 10015.

today: RFC 5288 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2008. It has been updated by RFC 9325 and RFC 10015, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: Why AES-GCM for TLS
sections.content:
RFC 5288 describes how to use the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in Galois Counter Mode (GCM) as a cipher suite for TLS. AES-GCM is an authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) cipher, as defined in TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246). It gives both confidentiality and data origin authentication in a single operation.

The RFC says the mode is efficient and secure, and that hardware implementations can reach high speeds with low cost and low latency because the mode can be pipelined. It also notes that AES-GCM is already specified for IPsec ESP (RFC 4106) and for 802.1AE MAC Security. Cipher suites based on elliptic curve cryptography are left to a separate document, RFC 5289.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one tool to hide a message and another to check it was not changed, this uses one fast tool that does both at once.

sections.title: The Twelve Cipher Suites
sections.content:
Section 3 defines twelve cipher suites, six pairs. In each pair one suite uses AES with a 128-bit key and the SHA-256 hash, and the other uses a 256-bit key and SHA-384. The pairs differ in the key exchange: RSA, DHE_RSA, DH_RSA, DHE_DSS, DH_DSS and DH_anon. The key exchanges themselves work as defined in RFC 5246.

The suites use the AEAD algorithms AEAD_AES_128_GCM and AEAD_AES_256_GCM from RFC 5116. Each uses a 128-bit authentication tag, and the RFC points out that the truncated_hmac extension has no effect on cipher suites that do not use HMAC.

IANA assigned the values {0x00,0x9C} through {0x00,0xA7}, in the order listed in the table below.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a menu of twelve ready-made recipes. Each one picks a lock size and a way for the two sides to agree on a secret.

sections.title: The GCM Nonce
sections.content:
AES-GCM needs a nonce, a value used once per encryption. Here the nonce SHALL be 12 bytes long and is made of two parts, a "partially explicit" nonce in the terms of RFC 5116: a salt of 4 bytes and a nonce_explicit of 8 bytes.

The salt is the implicit part. It is not sent in the packet. It comes from the handshake: it is the client_write_IV when the client is sending and the server_write_IV when the server is sending. The nonce_explicit is chosen by the sender and carried in each TLS record in the GenericAEADCipher.nonce_explicit field. It MAY be the 64-bit sequence number.

Each nonce_explicit value MUST be distinct for each invocation of the GCM encrypt function under a given key. Failing this can significantly degrade security.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message needs its own one-time number, like a ticket stub. Part of the number both sides already know, and the sender writes the rest on each message.

sections.title: PRF and Error Handling
sections.content:
The Pseudo Random Function (PRF) depends on the suite name. For suites ending in _SHA256 it is the TLS PRF from RFC 5246 with SHA-256 as the hash. For suites ending in _SHA384 it is the same PRF with SHA-384.

On errors, implementations MUST send the TLS alert bad_record_mac for all types of failures encountered while processing the AES-GCM algorithm. The RFC does not distinguish between kinds of failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The name of the recipe says which mixing method to use, and if anything goes wrong with a message, everyone says the same thing: it did not check out.

sections.title: TLS Versions
sections.content:
These suites rely on the authenticated encryption defined in TLS 1.2, so they MUST NOT be negotiated in older TLS versions. Clients MUST NOT offer them unless they also offer TLS 1.2 or later, and servers that select an earlier version MUST NOT select one of them.

TLS gives a client no way to say it supports TLS 1.2 but not earlier versions, so a non-compliant server might negotiate TLS 1.1 or earlier and still pick one of these suites. Clients MUST check the version and generate a fatal illegal_parameter alert if they see an incorrect one.
sections.plainLanguage: These recipes only work in the newer kitchen. If the old kitchen is picked by mistake, the client has to stop and say so.

sections.title: Counter Reuse and Multiple Processors
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5246 apply too. The main extra risk is that AES-GCM security requires the counter never be reused. The nonce construction in section 3 is designed to prevent that, and implementers should also read section 9 of the GCM specification on practical IV handling.

If a sender uses several cryptographic processors, it MUST make sure each nonce_explicit value under a given key is distinct. Each processor SHOULD put a fixed value that is distinct for that processor into the nonce_explicit, in the format FixedDistinct || Variable. All FixedDistinct fields MUST have the same length. The RFC's example uses salt eedc68dc with FixedDistinct values 01 and 02 for two processors.
sections.plainLanguage: If two helpers stamp tickets, give each helper their own first digit so they never print the same ticket number.

fields.name: salt
fields.desc: Implicit part, not sent; taken from the write IV set up in the handshake.

fields.name: nonce_explicit
fields.desc: Explicit part, chosen by the sender and carried in each TLS record.
